run.market_summary: 1) Rates are being repriced hawkishly. October payrolls beat (+165k, unemployment 4.1%) and pushed the odds of a December hike past 65%. October CPI is the next catalyst and the biggest risk this week. 2) The AI/semis trade is under pressure from two directions: the Jensen Huang personal scandal, which now carries a national-security angle, and post-election headlines saying the "AI trade" is getting hammered. Semis and the smaller AI cloud providers (CoreWeave, Nebius) are already down 9–16% in 5 days, so much of the move has happened. 3) The Middle East is escalating: Houthi strikes on Riyadh, a US strike near Qeshm, and the US rejecting Iran's ceasefire terms. But oil and energy stocks have fallen about 12% in a week and futures rallied on cheaper oil. The market isn't paying for the conflict, so I'm not betting against that price action. Overall I'm keeping few trades, because most candidates repeat the same rates bet or chase moves that have already happened.

ideas.thesis: Hot October jobs data (+165k, unemployment down to 4.1%) pushed December hike odds past 65%, yet TLT is flat over 5 days (+0.1%). Long bonds look under-priced for a hawkish Fed, and a firm CPI print would close that gap.

Nvidia has opened an internal investigation into Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and the BBC frames it as a national security issue. That creates real risk of a CEO change and more Washington scrutiny of China chip sales, on top of hawkish rates weighing on long-duration tech.

analysis.headline: Stocks had their best day since April 8 (S&P +2.35%, Dow +1,104) as last week's AI and semiconductor selloff reversed and oil fell about 4–6% on reports of a preliminary Iran deal. Nvidia was the exception, down 4.3% after its board opened a probe into Jensen Huang's alleged Chinese spy link.
analysis.narrative:
This was a broad relief rally after a bad week. All 13 sector ETFs rose, VIX fell 22%, and small caps (IWM +3.2%, z +2.2) and industrials (XLI +3.8%, z +3.0, the most unusual sector move) led. About 40% of the SPY move came at the open. The rest built during the session, and semiconductors made almost all of their gain after the open (SMH gap +0.2%, intraday +4.8%). That pattern points to dip-buying after a roughly 13% weekly drop in semis, not overnight news. UBS called the tech selloff "a positioning reset" around 1:48 pm, and Morgan Stanley and Jefferies also called it overdone. AMD (+13.3%, Oppenheimer upgrade to $600, EPYC chips hosting Google Cloud TPU systems), Broadcom (+8.8%), and chip-equipment names (AMAT +11.4% before its Nov 12 earnings, LRCX +10.4%) led. SOXX gained about 7.5%.

Nvidia went against the tape. It gapped down 7.3% on 3.9x normal volume after its board opened an independent investigation into Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, with bipartisan calls for testimony and talk of a tighter chip-export bill. It then recovered 3.25% during the session and closed down 4.3%, its worst lag versus peers since DeepSeek. Money moved out of NVDA and into AMD and AVGO, not out of AI chips altogether.

Oil was the second leg. Futures were already firmer before the open after Trump said renewed Iran strikes were "highly unlikely" if talks progress. In the afternoon, Saudi-owned outlets (Al Arabiya, Al Hadath) reported a preliminary uranium-enrichment deal brokered by Qatar and Pakistan. Neither Washington nor Tehran confirmed it, and a Qatari official disputed the details. WTI settled -4.4% at $86.85 and Brent -5.85% at $92.57. Reuters' close headline was "oil slide cools inflation worries." Airlines rose (JETS +5.2%) and energy lagged, the usual pattern for a supply story. The weekend's escalatory headlines (Houthi strike on the Aramco tower, a US strike near Qeshm, Rubio calling Iran's terms "outrageous") were ignored.

Rates did not join the rally. The 10-year was unchanged at 4.86% (down 2 bp at the open, up 3 bp during the session) with CPI due Tuesday and December hike odds above 65%. The dollar fell 0.55% (z -1.8) and gold rose 1.8%. A weaker dollar with higher gold and stocks looks like risk-on plus less inflation fear from oil, not a dovish repricing in bonds. With yields flat, the rally rested on positioning and oil, not on rates.

analysis.cross_asset_read: Risk-on, with VIX -22%, all sectors up, small caps and cyclicals leading, and the dollar down (z -1.8). The 10-year was flat at 4.86% with TLT unchanged, so this was not a rates rally. The bond market is holding its hawkish stance before CPI. Gold up with stocks and the dollar down fits easing inflation and oil fear plus a weaker USD, not a flight to safety. Oil down with airlines up and energy lagging oil's drop confirms a supply/geopolitics story. Inside tech, semis beating hyperscalers that gapped up and faded, with NVDA down while AMD and AVGO rallied, shows the move was rotation and short-covering within AI, not a new macro view. The Iran deal reports behind the oil drop were unconfirmed and disputed, so the oil move could reverse.

axis_realized.note: WTI -4.4% and Brent -5.85% on Trump's 'strikes unlikely' comment and Saudi-outlet reports of a preliminary Iran enrichment deal. Airlines rallied and energy lagged.
Markets traded on de-escalation hopes (deal reports, no renewed strikes) and ignored the Houthi/Aramco and Qeshm escalation headlines.
Reuters framed the rally as the oil slide cooling inflation worries. Yields did not confirm (10y flat), so the effect was weak.
The Huang spy probe raised export-bill and Washington-scrutiny risk, but the hit stayed on NVDA. The rest of semis rallied hard.

model_grade.summary: Mixed. The NVDA short paid (+4.3%), but all of that gain came from the gap, and NVDA rose 3.25% from the open. The model's main macro view (hawkish repricing) did not move prices: yields were flat and the dollar fell. It correctly said not to fight the falling-oil tape and that much of the AI selloff had already happened, but it did not act on that. It missed that last week's selloff would snap back in a large rally, and it missed the stock-specific catalysts (AMD, CAT).
got_right: NVDA as the AI name with idiosyncratic downside: -4.27%, about 6.6 points behind SPY
Saying the market was not paying for Middle East escalation: oil fell again and equities ignored the Houthi/Qeshm headlines
Saying the semis and neocloud selloff was largely done: semis bounced 7%+
got_wrong: monetary_policy +0.36 (hawkish) did not show up in prices: 10y flat, TLT +0.05%, dollar -0.55%, gold +1.8%
SHORT TLT was flat at best and lost badly against a +2.4% equity day
energy_supply +0.10 had the wrong sign: oil supply fears eased sharply (WTI -4.4%)
geopolitical_conflict +0.21: prices behaved as if the conflict was de-escalating
NVDA short entered at the open would have lost about 3.25%. The edge was all in the overnight gap.
missed: A broad relief rally of the kind that follows an oversold, positioning-driven selloff (S&P best day since April 8, all sectors up)
AMD Oppenheimer upgrade plus Google Cloud TPU win, and Broadcom's largest gain in a year
Caterpillar/Anthropic $3.4B generator order and industrials leading (XLI z +3.0)
Afternoon reports of a preliminary Iran deal that pushed oil to its lows

lessons: Discount the hawkish monetary_policy score when the jobs data is three days old and already priced (TLT flat for 5 days). Require new rates information (CPI, Fed speakers) before scoring it high or recommending duration shorts on a non-data day.
Check gap risk on company-scandal shorts: when the stock is already down more than 5% premarket, score the idea on the open-to-close move. Today NVDA closed down but rose 3.25% from the open.

When a sector has fallen more than 10% in 5 days on a narrative selloff (semis -13%, AI cloud names -50% in a month), weight a mean-reversion / long-peer idea (AMD, AVGO, equipment) instead of only fading the weakest name.

Set the sign of geopolitical_conflict and energy_supply from oil's own trend and diplomacy headlines (Trump 'strikes unlikely') more than from headline escalation counts. Oil -10% in 5 days was the better signal.
Flag single-name scandals as idiosyncratic: rivals can rally on share-shift (AMD/AVGO) instead of the whole sector selling off.
